stories.topic: Japan's Three Lost Decades of Zombies
stories.summary: After 1986, Japan's industrial policy, run by the Ministry of Finance and MITI, kept failing banks alive, and those banks kept failing firms alive. These artificially propped-up players went on competing with healthy firms and wiped out their profits, so the healthy firms could not invest. Ajay says this cost Japan thirty years of economic dynamism.
stories.insight: Refusing to let firms die is not mercy. The cost lands on the healthy firms, whose margins vanish and whose investment dries up. The bill is paid in decades of lost growth for the whole country.
stories.quote: Japan went through thirty years of misery because they had zombie banks which were keeping zombie firms aloft. The presence of these zombies shatters profitability for everybody else.

stories.topic: The Committee That Took Offence at 'Zombie Bank'
stories.summary: Years ago, on the Percy Mistry committee on Bombay as an international financial centre, Ajay and Percy kept using the term 'zombie bank'. Some committee members were offended and thought the word was disrespectful. Ajay explains it is a technical term that came out of the research on Japan.
stories.insight: Discomfort with precise, unsentimental words for failure is itself a symptom of the sentimentality that keeps zombies alive. Serious policy needs cold vocabulary.
stories.quote: Zombie firm, zombie banks are technical terms that have been introduced in the research on Japan.

stories.topic: The Bankruptcy Chapters That Never Made It Into the Companies Act
stories.summary: Montek Singh Ahluwalia, then deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, asked the Ministry of Company Affairs to put a full bankruptcy code, with collective negotiation among creditors, into the new Companies Act of 2013. The ministry assured him it would. It didn't. When Ajay later raised the issue, Montek asked whether he was sure it wasn't in there. Ajay had read the Act and found only trivial winding-up provisions.
stories.insight: Assurances from inside government are no substitute for someone who has actually read the law. Reform depends on people with the patience to check the fine print.
stories.quote: So when I first started these conversations with him, he said, Are you sure it's not there in the Companies Act 2013? And I said, I have done my fair share of bedtime reading.

stories.topic: How a Small Budget Paragraph Became the IBC
stories.summary: Ajay recounts KP Krishnan's story from The Seen and the Unseen. The 2015 budget speech had a paragraph from the MSME ministry promising a bankruptcy code for small companies. Krishnan asked Arun Jaitley whether they could go bigger and write a full code. Jaitley asked whether they had the ability and the teams. Krishnan pointed to FSLRC's large research teams and world-class law-drafting capability. That led to the BLRC, led by TK Viswanathan, with Susan Thomas and Ajay as members. Even then the initial vision was only to tweak the Companies Act's winding-up provisions. Rajiv Mehrishi, then Economic Affairs secretary, pushed for a full bankruptcy code instead. Susan's team wrote the first draft, and it became the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code in 2016.
stories.insight: Ambitious reform became possible only because capability had already been built (FSLRC). It also took a senior official willing to reject incrementalism.
stories.quote: And again at the beginning of the BLRC, there was a very narrow vision that, oh, we'll do some amendments to the winding up provisions of the Companies Act. And it was really a while before people got the point that no, a bankruptcy code is something playing at a different level. It's a negotiation mechanism for the creditors

stories.topic: 140 Sections Deleted, 8 Sections of SEBI Pasted In
stories.summary: The original draft of the bankruptcy law had about 140 sections setting out how to build the new regulator, the IBBI: checks and balances, separation of powers, governance. Ajay calls this the first time in India's history that regulator design got FSLRC-quality treatment. All of it was deleted. Someone pasted in roughly eight sections from the SEBI Act instead, importing SEBI's malfunctions into the IBBI.
stories.insight: Good institutional design can be lost in a single drafting decision. The quality of a reform depends on the unglamorous machinery of how its regulator is governed.
stories.quote: So all the bad practices of how SEBI malfunctions were brought into IBBI.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence Lessig
recommendations.context: Amit's pick at the end, prompted by the discussion of law and the 'shadow of the law'.
recommendations.reason: It is the first book that comes to his mind on the powerful impact of law and how every word matters. Lessig shows how law works like code, shaping how the rest of the machinery runs.

recommendations.reason: A collection of research papers on how the Indian bankruptcy reform was designed and how it has played out. This is the kind of research output Ajay says the field badly needs.

recommendations.reason: It is a live attempt to bring researchers together and rebuild the knowledge ecosystem that Ajay says has dissipated.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything's episodes on firms: Ep 21 The Beauty of Finance, Ep 34 How Family Firms Evolve, Ep 37 From Imperial to Adaptive Firms, Ep 48 Graduating to Globalisation

recommendations.context: Amit lists them in the intro as the earlier episodes this one builds on.
recommendations.reason: Together they cover the life of firms: a foundational history of finance (an episode Amit says he 'absolutely loves'), how family firms should evolve, when firms should centralise or decentralise, and going global. This episode adds the death of firms.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit recalls it while explaining why central planning cannot meet society's needs.
recommendations.reason: It covers the papers on why firms exist and how the price system works from the bottom up. That is the intellectual background for letting markets, not planners, decide which firms survive.

recommendations.creator: Ronald Coase
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it as 'a paper talking about firms' from the Four Papers episode.
recommendations.reason: The foundational answer to what a firm is, which this episode takes for granted.

recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Amit mentions Hayek's paper on the price system.
recommendations.reason: It explains how markets let people meet each other's needs from the bottom up, which central planning cannot do in a complex, changing world.

recommendations.reason: It lays out the pipeline of data, research, rival proposals and public criticism that any policy reform needs. Ajay argues this pipeline has broken down for bankruptcy.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay invokes how he and Vijay Kelkar 'zero-base' the essential functions of the state; the book is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Background for the episode's argument that a few fundamentals of state capability must come first.

core_ideas.concept: Creative Destruction Needs Both Vishnu and Shiva
core_ideas.explanation: Schumpeter's story: innovators take risks and earn a temporary monopoly rent on a new idea, and that prospect motivates research and business-model innovation. Meanwhile, old firms that can't keep up go bankrupt. Their labour and capital aren't lost; they flow to other firms, the way your atoms return to other forms of life. Ajay maps this onto the Hindu triad of creation, preservation and destruction: interfere with any one and the balance breaks. The bankruptcy process is the Shiva.
core_ideas.quote: So it's just like you know, the carbon and the hydrogen atoms inside you will go back into other forms of life. So there's a ceaseless concept of firm destruction and firm creation, and that's a normal and healthy part of society.

core_ideas.concept: A Firm Is a Recipe, Like DNA
core_ideas.explanation: A firm takes labour and capital and organises them in particular ways, like DNA assembling molecules into a creature. It is easy to get emotional about a firm, but the recipe can be bad, or the world can move on. Some firms reinvent themselves: Tata Steel today is unrecognisable from Jamshedji Tata's original. Most don't, and they should go out of business.
core_ideas.quote: It is easy to become emotional about a creature. But it can happen that that recipe is not a great one, or that the world moves on, the world changes.

core_ideas.concept: Complexity and Flux Rule Out Central Planning
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's two axioms: the world is complex, and the world is always changing. So society's needs can only be met by bottom-up processes like markets. Profit rewards serving others, and adaptation is simply learning to keep serving them. A firm that fails to adapt should exit, so its labour and resources can be better used elsewhere.
core_ideas.quote: What is adaptation? Adaptation is learning how to keep serving other people in society.

core_ideas.concept: Limited Liability Is a Cold Contract
core_ideas.explanation: Since the company was invented in 15th–16th century Europe, shareholders control the firm only while they service their debts. Creditors have no say until a default. Then a judge only has to confirm that there was credit and there was a default. Shareholders are thrown out and usually wiped out, and the creditors take control under a reconstructed balance sheet. Operational creditors such as unpaid suppliers are creditors just as much as lenders. Ajay laments that Indians get sentimental about promoter families instead of understanding these definitional basics.
core_ideas.quote: It's a very dramatic fact about the concept of a limited liability company, that shareholders are in charge of the company as long as they are meeting their dues. The day the shareholders fail to pay their dues, they're supposed to get thrown out and replaced by the creditors.

core_ideas.explanation: Firms that are 'dead men walking', kept alive by more debt from badly regulated banks or by government pressure, compete with healthy firms and destroy their margins. Healthy firms that aren't profitable can't invest, so dynamism dies across the economy. Ajay's example: a propped-up Air India or Jet Airways selling cheap tickets hurts a quality airline like Vistara. Clearing out the weak creates the profitability that makes the strong invest more.
core_ideas.quote: These firms that are dead men walking are called zombie firms. By the way, by symmetry, the banks that are dead men walking are called zombie banks.

core_ideas.concept: A Failing Firm Is a Melting Ice Cube
core_ideas.explanation: Once trouble starts, insiders know first. Key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, maintenance is skipped, and promoters with better information may start siphoning cash. Delay destroys value and gives bad actors more time. So the ideal system has an objective early warning and a fast bankruptcy process. Business failure should carry no stigma: in a risk-taking world, firms should go bankrupt, with a well-defined script for what follows.
core_ideas.quote: Once a firm starts getting into trouble, it's a melting ice cube. It rapidly falls apart.

core_ideas.concept: Going Concern vs. Liquidation Is a Business Judgment
core_ideas.explanation: A firm is more than its factory and offices. Its people, processes, IT systems, culture and external relationships form intangible capital, which is often worth a lot. Caught early, a firm is usually worth more as a going concern sold to a new owner than chopped up and liquidated. Caught late, the intangibles are gone and liquidation is all that's left. Creditors must compare the options coldly ('will I get 40 or 70?') without humanitarian sentiment.
core_ideas.quote: I want to emphasize that this is not a value judgment. This is not any humanitarian notion that oh we should protect the company as a going concern. This is a business judgment.

core_ideas.concept: The Committee of Creditors Needs Commercial Badasses
core_ideas.explanation: After default, all creditors become a committee holding the shareholders' powers. A supermajority (say 60–70%), not a bare majority, must agree. They haggle. A secured creditor holding a critical factory can threaten to torpedo a going-concern plan unless paid well. Bids are often not all-cash: a promise to repay over 20 years from an untested bidder versus a solid 80 from an industry player is a qualitative call. India tends to treat it like government procurement, because its bureaucratic, over-regulated financial firms lack commercial instinct.
core_ideas.quote: What we want is a badass commercially sophisticated committee of creditors that is able to view these risks and make deals and do negotiations and come up with a value maximizing answer.

core_ideas.concept: Banks Hide Bad News, So Cut Their Votes
core_ideas.explanation: Indian banks' overriding goal is to avoid recognising losses. The loan stays on the books at 100, and evergreening (lending again so the borrower can repay) kicks the can down the road. PSU and even private banks worry about future CBI investigations and 'paint the tape' to look good. They prefer one-on-one renegotiation in darkness to the open committee of creditors, and on committees they delay ('let's meet next month'). Ajay's unorthodox fix: until banking regulation improves, reduce banks' voting power relative to more commercial players like mutual funds, FIIs, NBFCs, insurers and operational creditors.
core_ideas.quote: You know, one day banks will get their act right, banking regulation will get its act right. In the meantime, maybe what you should do is give them less voting power

core_ideas.concept: Should Promoters Bid for Their Own Firm?
core_ideas.explanation: India bars promoters from bidding once bankruptcy begins. Ajay thinks that is mostly a mistake, because promoters know every corner of the business and might bid highest. The stronger counter-argument is 'poison pills': a promoter who knows she can return could plant hidden landmines, such as odd contract provisions, that only she can defuse, scaring off other bidders. Given weak rule of law, such acts don't land people in jail. So promoters are fully excluded, while banks quietly restructure loans with them in secret. Neither is a market-based auction.
core_ideas.quote: Now I think that's a mistake. So I think it's a healthy thing that it's a competitive process. Many people can come in with offers to the committee of creditors, and the promoter should be permitted to be one of them.

core_ideas.concept: India's IBC Is a C-Grade Project
core_ideas.explanation: The design was sound, but the environment drags it down. Bureaucratic banks dominate committees. The NCLT works like any other slow Indian court, though its job should take days. The IBBI lost its carefully designed governance sections. Insolvency professionals and others face corrupt pressures under weak rule of law. Contrast the UK, where bankruptcy practice evolved for centuries as self-organising market practice before being codified, while India waits for a regulator to write rules.
core_ideas.quote: India has a C grade bankruptcy process. Okay, like it's there and yeah, it's better to have it than not to have it, but it has many difficulties.

core_ideas.concept: Inputs, Outputs, Outcomes and the Shadow of the Law
core_ideas.explanation: Judge a policy by outcomes. In education, schools are inputs, grades are outputs, and learning is the outcome. In bankruptcy, the law, NCLT and committees are inputs, and resolved cases and recoveries are outputs. The outcome we want is a better credit market where borrowers are keen to repay and lenders keen to lend, so leverage should rise. In advanced economies most disputes never reach court; they are settled privately because everyone knows what the law would do. Amit adds that 'the law' here means the whole invisible infrastructure of enforcement and state capability, not just the statute.
core_ideas.quote: So the term used is in the shadow of the law. Only a few cases go. Because you're not able to find the correct negotiation. Most cases, actually, the behavior of all counterparties is changed.

core_ideas.explanation: Passing a law and setting up a regulator is only the beginning of iterative refinement. That requires data sets, researchers, working papers, blog posts, op-eds and criticism, so that officials have something to act on. Without criticism, ministers assume everything is fine. India briefly had a bankruptcy research community, then it dissipated. Policy-support consultancies supplying English-speaking young staff to joint secretaries are a staffing arrangement, not intellectual leadership.
core_ideas.quote: It's an embarrassment that there's probably two papers in this field coming out a year. There ought to be like twenty papers on this field coming out every year.

core_ideas.explanation: From 1991 to 2011 many reforms moved at once: capital controls, equity markets, software, telecom. Each strengthened the others. With few projects moving, there is little positive feedback. The bankruptcy reform suffered because the banking regulation reform that should have run alongside it never happened. A good law in weak infrastructure may underperform now but improve as other pieces fall into place. Sometimes, though, it is wiser to settle for a compromise suited to present conditions.
core_ideas.quote: So when many, many policy projects are moving, it's actually a virtuous cycle, it strengthens everything.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay and Vijay Kelkar ask which public-policy elements are essential for civilisation and a market economy. Their list: foreign policy, military, fiat money, criminal justice, police and courts, a tax system to pay for them, and some commercial law and financial regulation. Since reformers, researchers and philanthropic capital are scarce, they should concentrate on these core pillars rather than be spread across every worthy cause.
core_ideas.quote: Give me a list of the elements of the state, of public policy, that are essential for civilization, that without that, you will be in barbarism.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'Firms are awesome, firms are amazing, firms are edifying, firms are illuminating, and when firms are sexually aroused, firms are firm.'
After Ajay invokes Vishnu and Shiva to explain creative destruction, Amit asks: 'Am I sitting with Ajay Shah or am I sitting with my friend Devdutt Pattanaik?'

Ajay credits 'the great Amit Varma' for telling creators to throw things at the wall. Amit admits he gave that advice to a friend starting a vlog, and five minutes later the friend called back to say the camera broke. 'So this is not always great advice.'

Amit: 'Japan not only had zombie firms and zombie banks, she also made a lot of great zombie movies.' He wonders whether to rewatch them for hidden metaphor: 'dead man walking, axe in hand, hand chopped off, ha ha ha. But actually perhaps there's something deeper going on there.'
Amit, recalling the early Seen and the Unseen episodes: 'My memory is pretty close to being a zombie, so I'm not quite sure of this.'
Ajay on why stakeholder-talk has no place in bankruptcy: 'The word stakeholder is a sure sign of feeble reasoning. What is needed here is cold business reasoning.'
Ajay's backhanded compliment to Indian lenders, who eventually wise up to promoters who misbehave: 'The credit markets in India are medium foolish. They are not deeply foolish.'
Amit asks how bankers can judge a failed biscuit factory. Ajay: 'They gave you hundred crore rupees... At that time, they're bloody well going to understand your industry.'
Amit pictures a promoter's poison pill as 'a rat trap in the corner office under the chair under the table.' Ajay: 'Correct. That's literally what can be done.'
After Ajay grades the IBC he helped create as C-grade, Amit teases: it makes him 'deeply sad' that the work of Ajay, Susan and Bhargavi 'is today being dismissed by some random uncle as third rate.'
On banks preferring to renegotiate one creditor at a time, in darkness, rather than in the open committee: 'Sunlight is the best disinfectant.'

Ajay on India's policy-support consultancies: 'It's a staffing arrangement that you get a young person that speaks perfect English to work for the joint secretary. And that's not going to give intellectual leadership.'
Amit trips over the word 'internationalization' and settles on the geek shorthand: 'I eighteen N.'
Joseph Schumpeter's creative destruction: innovators earn a temporary monopoly rent on new ideas, while firms that can't keep up go bankrupt.
Douglass North and Oliver Williamson: Ajay cites their view that institutions create the conditions for people to enter into complex contracts, which is what bankruptcy machinery does.
Japan's Ministry of Finance and MITI: their industrial policy orchestrated the zombie banks and zombie firms behind Japan's lost decades.
Air India, Jet Airways and Vistara: Ajay's example of propped-up airlines driving down ticket prices and hurting a high-quality competitor.
Tata Steel: today's company is 'unrecognizably different' from Jamshedji Tata's original, proof that an old dog can learn new tricks.

India's road to the IBC: the SARFAESI Act (2002) gave secured creditors rights to seize collateral but pushed everything toward liquidation. The Companies Act 2013 had only trivial winding-up provisions. FSLRC under Justice Srikrishna (2011–2015) built bankruptcy machinery for financial firms. The BLRC under TK Viswanathan drafted the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016.

In the UK, bankruptcy practice evolved for hundreds of years out of common sense, common law and market practice before it was ever codified. Ajay calls it a self-organising system that 'groped and found these institutions'.
The insolvency professional who runs a bankruptcy case is described as 'a bit of a maître d'' overseeing the whole process.
